title: Measuring the Quantum Signature of Relational Time on Superconducting Hardware
description:
An experimental program testing whether relational time — time defined by correlations between a clock and the rest of a system rather than by an external parameter — leaves a measurable quantum signature distinguishable from its classical mimic.

Thirteen pre-registered runs on IBM Quantum Heron processors (ibm_marrakesh, ibm_fez), 74 jobs, 706 circuits of raw counts archived across 36 jobs with server-side provenance and backend calibration for every run and zero empty calibration records.

  • IBM-0: the conditional-evolution signal usually cited as “time from entanglement” is reproduced by a classical clock control to within shot noise; the clock-marginal coherence witness is not, scales with clock dimension, and vanishes at a structural null. Replicated across two devices.
  • IBM-1: the witness has a measured decoherence threshold following a power law in the clock-record overlap; conditional evolution survives at R² ≥ 0.94 at every coupling strength, including where the witness has collapsed — apparent temporal dynamics outliving its own quantum signature.
  • IBM-2: that witness is necessary but not sufficient — a coherent clock–system product state with zero entanglement scores 1.9–4.2× higher on it.
  • IBM-3: the joint-readout replacement fails the same way (a separable mixture scores 1.7× higher), and a two-line theorem shows no functional of a single local product-basis measurement setting can certify clock–system entanglement.
  • IBM-4: a multi-setting fidelity witness does certify it — F = 0.9419 (d=4) and 0.8829 (d=8) against a derived separable bound of 0.5, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals clearing the bound outright and both adversarial states correctly rejected by the same measurement.
  • IBM-5: the global state is stationary — invariant under the joint clock-shift-plus-evolution but not under either factor alone nor the mismatched pairing (44–167σ at d=4) — and the operator that makes it stationary is the same one generating its conditional dynamics.
  • IBM-6, IBM-8: reported as failures. Both spent shots measuring a quantity fixed by construction; published unclosed, and the source of the standing preflight rule that governs every later run.
  • IBM-7, IBM-9: a hardware-measured commensurability condition for exact cycle closure of a finite cyclic clock, and coherent superposition of two programmed relational rates producing interference of 0.2411 where every classical rate mixture predicts exactly zero.
  • IBM-10: entangled, stationary as a ray, and internally evolving measured on a single preparation in a single job — the mechanism's actual content, rather than three properties of three states.
  • IBM-11: the marginal witness does not merely fail to certify entanglement — it runs backwards. Swept from a product state to a Bell pair, witness and CHSH anti-correlate at r = -0.9573, and the witness-maximising state produces no Bell violation at all (CHSH 1.8605, below the classical bound).
  • IBM-12: what shared relational time costs. Moving a clock's entanglement partner from its own system to a second clock, clock quality trades against synchronisability at r = -0.9833 with both endpoints reaching exactly zero — a clock maximally entangled with its own system has no measurable correlation with any other clock. At the balance point neither pair violates Bell.

The two closing runs close a class. IBM-11 measures the P = 0 slice of the Jakob-Bergou complete complementarity relation (Phys. Rev. A 68, 022107, 2003); IBM-12 measures Coffman-Kundu-Wootters monogamy (Phys. Rev. A 61, 052306, 2000). Both identities are standard and neither is claimed here — but they are the same conserved unit, spent once against a clock's own local coherence and once against every partner other than its own system, and depolarizing noise never creates headroom in either. A Page-Wootters clock earns its quality by spending that budget on itself, so no correlation magnitude can serve as a shared temporal reference between two good clocks — a property of the observable class, not a limitation of this apparatus. What the budget does not cover is quantities that are not magnitudes: the Aharonov-Anandan geometric phase depends on the path in projective Hilbert space and is reparameterisation-invariant, which is the invariance a time shared between clocks of different rates would require. Whether it too is on the budget is open and is the specified next run.

Also archived: the preceding cross-datacenter TPU telemetry experiments (disciplined nulls, with the raw 128 Hz streams), the synthetic Page-Wootters / D-LinOSS simulation campaign from which the hypothesis and the measurement-diversity certification standard originate, and a Bose-Einstein-condensate entropic-time bridge that failed its pre-registered gate.

Every limitation was found by this program's own pre-registered adversarial controls. All raw shot counts, pre-registrations, and server-side provenance (job IDs, calibration snapshots) are archived; every analysis reproduces from counts without IBM access.

Claim boundary: nothing here claims that time in nature is emergent, tests quantum gravity or the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, or realizes a physical Page-Wootters universe. The history state is engineered by externally timed gates, the clock/system split is imposed rather than derived, the certification is device-dependent, and the clock is 2-5 qubits. Endpoints measured at exactly zero are statements about correlation between engineered registers, not about simultaneity in nature.

Simulation phase supported by Google TPU Research Cloud; hardware phase by the IBM Quantum Open Plan.
